tip: Present-tense 'volta' covers near-future plans, so 'Quando você volta?' means when are you coming back, not just when do you return now.
'A gente' literally means the people but works as informal we, and it takes third-person singular: 'a gente se encontra', never encontramos.
Gostar always takes 'de' before what you like, so it is 'gosto de cozinhar' even though English 'like cooking' has no preposition.
'Fazer da vida' is the everyday way to ask about someone's job, so 'O que você faz da vida?' asks what you do for a living.
The impersonal 'se' in 'como se diz' means how does one say, with no specific subject, the normal way to ask for a word.
'Estão cheias' uses estar because crowded is the streets' condition right now, not a permanent trait; ser would sound inherent.
For -ar verbs the nós form is identical in present and past, so 'jantamos' can mean we dine or we dined, and context decides.
Gostar always needs 'de' where English 'like' takes no preposition: it is 'gosta de acordar', and dropping the de breaks it.
'São fartos' uses ser because generous portions are the inherent character of mineira cooking, not a passing state.
The superlative frame is 'o mais alto da família', where Portuguese says of the family where English says in the family.
Unlike Spanish gustar, Portuguese gostar keeps normal order: subject plus 'gostam de churrasco', with no subject flip.
'Ainda bem' is literally still well and works as thank goodness, so 'Ainda bem que deu certo' expresses relief.
'A gente' means we but takes third-person singular, so it is 'a gente gosta', never gostamos.
After 'de' Portuguese uses the plain infinitive where English uses -ing, so 'gosta de ler' means likes reading.
The circumflex is the only difference between 'pôde' (was able, past) and 'pode' (can, present), so watch the accent.
'Nada a ver' is literally nothing to see, but it means nothing to do with it, a common way to reject a claim.
'Simpático' means nice or friendly, not English sympathetic; that sense is 'compreensivo'.
Portuguese puts 'de' before the infinitive where English says forget to, so it is 'esqueci de comprar', not esqueci comprar.
Use 'por' for a span of time: 'por dois anos' means for two years, and para there would wrongly signal purpose.
Physical traits are treated as permanent, so they take ser: 'Ele é gordo e baixo', never estar.
'Esperávamos' is imperfect painting the ongoing scene, while 'nevou' is preterite marking the single event that happened.
After a superlative Portuguese uses de, not em: 'a melhor pizza da cidade' means the best pizza in the city.
Here 'se' is reciprocal, so 'todo mundo se conhecia' means everyone knew each other, not everyone knew themselves.
In 'ir à praia' the à is the preposition a plus the article a squeezed together, and the grave accent is the only visible sign.
Portuguese takes breakfast rather than has it: 'tomaram café da manhã' uses the same tomar you use for drinks.
Adjectives usually follow the noun, so it is 'emprego novo', not novo emprego.
'Há' before a time span means ago, so 'há seis meses' means six months ago.
'Fazer questão de' means to insist on, literally to make a point of, so 'fez questão de pagar' means he insisted on paying.
'A gente' means we but takes a singular verb: 'a gente chegou', never chegamos.
Portuguese changes of something: 'mudar de ideia' means change your mind, and the de is required, like mudar de casa.
In the preterite querer marks a completed act of wanting or trying, so 'a gente quis ajudar' means we tried to help.
'Estava dormindo' is the imperfect ongoing background, and 'tocou' is the preterite event that interrupts it.
'Perguntou se' means asked whether: se introduces an indirect question, reporting it rather than quoting it.
'Que' plus a noun makes what a, so 'Que pena' means what a shame, the same shape as que sorte or que legal.
Portuguese makes a trip rather than takes one: 'fez uma viagem' means took a trip, using fazer instead of tomar.
'Curtir' is informal Brazilian for enjoy or have fun, so 'curtiu a praia' means enjoyed the beach.
'A tempo' means just in time, while 'no prazo' means by the deadline, so 'terminou a tempo' means finished with time to spare.
For this -ir verb the nós form is the same in present and past, so 'dividimos' can mean we split or we are splitting.
Portuguese makes friendship rather than becomes friends, so 'fez amizade com' means became friends with.
'Experimentar' looks like experiment but means to try, especially food, so 'experimentaram o açaí' means did you try the açaí.
Don't confuse 'viemos' (we came) with vimos (we saw); they are different verbs that sound close.
'Combinar de' plus an infinitive means to arrange or agree to, so 'combinou de se encontrar' means arranged to meet.
In the preterite saber shifts to found out, so 'soube da notícia' means I found out the news, not I already knew it.
'Dar uma olhada' is literally to give a look and means to take a look, so 'deram uma olhada' means did you take a look.
'Voltamos' is both present and past for this verb; here 'ontem' is what tells you it means we came back yesterday.
'A gente' means we but takes third-person singular: 'a gente viajou', never viajamos.
